en: The *Rasārṇava-sudhākara* of Siṃhabhūpāla. Abbreviations used:
*amaru.* = *Amaru-śatakam*.
A.Rā. = Anargha-rāghava; Bā.Rā. = Bāla-rāmāyaṇa;
Bha.Nā.Śā. = Bharata-nāṭya-śāstra.
bhā.pra. = Bhāvaprakāśikā (by Śaradātanaya) ha.nā. = Hanumannāṭakaḥ (Karuṇākandala)
Kā.ā. = *Kāvyādarśa*; Ku.ā. = *Kuvalayānanda* (Siṃhabhūpāla);
Ku.saṃ. = *Kumārasambhava* (Kālidāsa).
*Kṛ.ka.* = *Kṛṣṇakarṇāmṛta* (Līlāśuka); *Gāthā* = *Gāthāsaptasatī*;
*Mā.mā.* = *Mālatīmādhava*.
Mā.ā.mi. = Mālavikāgnimitra;
Śi.va. = Śiśupālavadha (by Māgha);
Me.dū. = Meghadūta or Meghasandeśa.
*Nāgā* = *Nāgānanda*,
*Ra.ā.* = *Ratnāvalī* (by Śrīharṣa), *Ra.vaṃ.* = *Raghuvamśaḥ* (by Kālidāsa).
Sa.ka.ā. = *Sarasvatī-kaṇṭhābharaṇa* (Bhoja);
Śaku. or A.Śa. = *Abhijñāna-śākuntala* (Kālidāsa);
U.Rā.Ca. = *Uttara-rāma-carita*.
vai.śa. = Vairāgya-śataka of Bhartṛhari; vi.u. = Vikramorvaśīya;
vi.pu. = Viṣṇu-purāṇa.
Ve.Saṃ. = Veṇīsaṃhāra by Nārāyaṇabhaṭṭa; Rasārṇavasudhākara composed by Śrī Siṃhabhūpāla (1).
The First Vilāsa: The Exaltation of the Enchanter;
the Friendship of the Erotic and the Heroic; the Fragrance of Innocence and Boldness.
We worship that conjugal union which possesses the grace of the *lāsya* and *tāṇḍava* dances.
I ever revere Sarasvatī, whose hand is marked by a lute, who has the eyes of a doe,
who is composed of eternal bliss, and who is the beloved of the goddess seated upon the lotus.
There exists a certain supreme reality, the sprout of ultimate bliss, the space between the arms of one who is curious about the firmness of Kamalā’s breasts.
From his lotus feet was born a lineage free from all stain,
which attained the status of being a brother to the fruit of Bhagīratha’s ascetic penance.
There, in the ocean of the Recarla lineage, there was a leader named Dācaya, who was like the full moon of the autumnal night, a treasury of artistic talents, and possessed of noble splendor.
By means of the path of his sword’s edge, though it was difficult to traverse,
the Goddess of Victory came from the host of Pandya kings' elephants onto the battlefield.
In that Aṅganārāyaṇa, whose sovereignty was exceedingly firm,
the earth became like a submissive female elephant under the goad of a wicked royal tusker.
His wife was highly fortunate and renowned like Śrī herself;
she was the noble Poyyamāmbā, born of a lineage as venerable as the lotus.
To those two were born three sons, who were like wish-fulfilling trees for the earth and who terrified the heroic warriors of their enemies:
Siṃhaprabhu, Vennamanāyaka, and [the third].
The foremost of heroes and the lord of the earth are both *reca*.

In this Kali age, Dharma, which consists of but a single foot, has attained the state of being complete in all its four feet through these [virtues] that act like its steps; thus, it no longer yearns for the Kṛta Yuga.
While Siṃha was protecting the entire earth as its sovereign,
it was a marvel that the kings who bowed down experienced exaltation, while those who did not bow down experienced humiliation.
In the vicinity of Kṛṣṇeśvara, at Mel̥eśvara where great preparations had been made, that Lord repeatedly performed the consecration of Brahmins without any obstacle;
by means of his various personal qualities, he attained freedom from debt to them.
In Brahmā, who is occupied with the weight of the exertion required for his extraordinary creative emanations.
Seeing his sword, crooked as the tongue of Death, the enemies who trembled felt a surge of sweat arise within their gathered hearts.
It brings about the pacification of the heat of pride.
The illustrious Reca-Mahīpati, whose younger brother Su-carita clearly attained the even greater renown of being a "teacher of heroes" (vīra-guru)— a title that serves as the hallmark of a hero—
having acquired the honorific title "Lord of the Kathāris" (Labdha-Kaṭhāri-Rāya) marked by the sign of Rāhuttara.
[He saw] his son, the leader of the Naga race, the unique crest-jewel of the heroes of the earth.
This very Siṃhamahīpāla is clearly Vasudeva,
whose two sons, Ananta and Mādhava, are the protectors of the world.
Therein was his younger brother, Mādhava-nāyakendra, whose majesty was renowned throughout the quarters of the world;
from him there arose kings who were the founders of dynasties.
The foremost mountains of the Vedas became attenuated.
His elder brother, because his affection for the earth was not diminished by the faults of kings, bore the well-known name Anapota,
which was true to its literal meaning.
And the perception of infinity, as well as the state of being a mountain.
He whose brother is Balabhadra by nature, whose beloved queen is Rukmiṇī, whose son is Pradyumna, and whose multitude of grandsons includes Aniruddha and others—
he is this very Lord of Śrī, King Annapota; moreover, [he resides] upon the lotus of his own face.
And he bears the beautiful splendor of the Sudarśana [discus] upon the lotus-hand of his own being.
Having made the earthly realm protected by many sons of Soma,
Hari feels ashamed while protecting the heavenly realm with only one son of Soma.
While the one who is a Paraśurāma to the Soma clan,
terrifying in the strength of his arms, and a cowherd to the enemies of the Aryan race,
remains awake and rules there.
It eternally awakens the constant welfare of the worlds.
Having placed a golden mountain within the reach of the gods on earth through gifts of gold,
he who fashioned it with a path of beautiful stairs—
Śrīparvata, accessible by the feet of all people.
It is marvelous that he who is the destroyer of many heroes, though numbering the infinite, has never broken his own course of action,
and though his existence is free from the confusion of birth.
It bears the mark of Bhārgava, who is of the lineage of Soma.
As enemy kings, cast down upon the field of battle, ran and ran,
they beheld him before them with his body reflected in every sword;
though they turned back from there and looked hither and thither, [they could not find him].
They clearly and unerringly recognize him as one who bears the marks of a rhinoceros and Nārāyaṇa.
The queen of that lord of the earth was renowned as Annamāmbā, resplendent like Śivā, the consort of Śiva, to that crest-jewel among kings. (SRs 1.24)
Śrutakīrti gladdens Śatrughna, and Subhadrā, dark-complexioned and radiant, brings joy to her husband, the illustrious King Arjuna.
To those two were born two sons: the first was Veda-girīśvara, and the second was that peerless King Siṃha by virtue of his fame.
Then the illustrious King Siṃha, long-lived, will place this earth firmly and without artifice upon the seat of his own shoulders. (1.27)
With the binding of the bowstring unslackened, with a supreme bow as radiant as gold,
with arrows that destroy the enemy's strength, and with many hostile cities as his domain—
thus, for the most part, by means of this method of preparation for a superhuman battle.
This Maheśa is the one whom people call the Lion-King.
And wherein there was the girding on of armor for battle,
the departure from one's own city with grass in hand,
and the wandering in the forest— that very conduct [is what is meant].
Or attending upon those who are one's enemies as a refuge. //SRs_1.29//
Bringing joy to the virtuous, causing the blue water-lilies to bloom,
nourishing lovely arts, and even embodying the story of the physician Jīvātṛka—
oh, how this king most fully manifests the rising of a friend!
Likewise, [he experiences] the bliss of the *cakra*s and the exquisite splendor of the blossoming lotus.
Indeed, those drops of water obtained from the dense clouds by the ocean attain the state of pearls only when they enter oyster shells during the constellation Svāti;
for it was only when the droplets of the water of their gifts fell into the hands of the wise that they became [pearls].
Rubies, magnificent garments, many dwellings, and gold.
Having recognized that this [king] possesses policy as his virtue and that his own position is devoid of virtue, the enemy kings—
[those who were once] experts in the virtues of policy toward him— [fled].
They bow down until their foreheads reach the surface of his lotus feet.
"Your subordinate kings, having repeatedly sought refuge in my livelihood for the sake of preserving their lives, ought to be protected by you out of compassion"—
thus did his most intimate friends whisper into his ear as it rested against the edge of his ear.
I believe that the wish-granting cow (Kāmadhenu) has taken refuge in the vicinity of the corners of his eyes.

When the enemies arrived, those women— having mastered the art of responding to the shifting expressions on their faces— spoke out of a sense of shame prompted by the inquiries of the inner apartments as to how they had protected their lives during the battle with Pratigaṇḍabhairava.
The sprouts of the color of ruby-jewels shine from their swaying earrings upon their ears.
Like the Mandāra, Pārijātaka, Candana, Santāna, Kalpavṛkṣa, and Cintāmaṇi trees,
he was a beloved who never abandoned those seeking refuge.
[They were] known by the names Veda, Giri, Svāmin, Māda, Dāma, and Ya.
He who shines upon this earth like a mine of jewels, possessing his own vast riches and rejoicing in giving that is not easily obtained by other people.
The exquisite splendor of his lotus-like feet was fashioned by the rays of the king’s crown.
He whose first elder brother was the illustrious Annapota, a crest-jewel among princes distinguished by his virtues; who surpassed the elder brother of one [his own] in personal beauty and wealth,
and the elder brother of two in the prowess of his irresistible arms when he had ascended the bow— [that king] reigns supreme.
In truthfulness he was like the four-faced Brahmā, and in generosity even like the five-faced Śiva.
In battle, the rival kings, scorched by the heat of his valor, sink into the water of the edge of the sword-blade of that lord Kumāradāsa;
yet it is a marvel that his wives have their *tilaka* marks vanished and their dark tresses disheveled.
The saffron from their breasts was falling away, and the black collyrium at the corners of their eyes was trickling down.
In him, who nourishes his jewel-like son,
the beloved Vallabharāja, that full moon,
there arises for the virtuous a remnant of spiritual power.
But the blossoming of lotuses is indeed a marvel. //SRs_1.39//
Together with these and other sons, this very Lion-King attains stability through six [sons], just as a master does through his well-united limbs.
That king occupied the capital named Rājācala, which had come down through the succession of his lineage;
therein he provided protection for the virtuous and instruction for the wicked.
Those who possess knowledge follow [the truth] in accordance with logic.
Protecting the circle of the earth between the Vindhya and Śrīśaila mountains with his sons who continue the lineage, this Indra among enjoyers partakes of all worldly objects.
While that son of Annapota, who delighted in the land like a lion, was ruling the earth,

sovereignty that surpasses all others is declared to be great fortune.

The beloved woman, longing for her lover who is dear to her heart and yet delayed in returning,
is unable even to look at honey, sandalwood, or a mango tree;
she does not even notice that the bracelet has slipped from her hand, its pearls having fallen away.
Hearing the cry of the cuckoo, she sheds tears and trembles.
Now, as for the *khaṇḍitā*:
she whose lover, having transgressed their agreement and enjoyed another woman, adorned with the marks of that enjoyment, returns in the morning—she indeed is the *khaṇḍitā*. (1.219)
But for this [woman], anxiety, sighing, silence, shedding tears, exhaustion, confusion, indistinct speech, and so forth are considered the physical transformations [of love]. (1.220)
As in my own verse:
"At dawn, having seen her lord of her life with his body marked by the fresh seal of passion, the young bride repeatedly utters something crooked in anger."
Now he gives way to anxiety, now he wanders about, now he lets out a sigh, and now he sheds tears.
Now, regarding the woman separated by a quarrel (*kalahāntaritā*):
she who, having angrily repulsed her beloved as he fell at her feet before her friends, later feels remorse—that indeed is the *kalahāntaritā*. (SRs 1.222)
Furthermore, her delusions, incoherent talk, fainting, sighing, fever, and frequent lamentation—these and other such symptoms are recognized by the wise as the desired signs [of love]. (1.223)
As in my own verse:
"Having utterly cast aside her lover who was prostrate at her feet, the beloved, now free from hesitation, speaks in distress to her friend today: 'What have I done that you are so angry?'"
She wanders about in agitation, casting her restless and troubled gaze in every direction; she repeatedly loathes what is lovely, prattles on, breathes heavily, and faints away. (SRs 1.224)
Now, the *abhisārikā* (one's own woman) is she who, tormented by the fire of love, goes to meet her beloved;
she is radiant with moonlight, dressed in dark garments, and adorned with ornaments suitable for the journey. (1.225)
She who goes out to meet her lover herself is known as an *abhisārikā*;
her transformations, such as longing and anxiety, should be portrayed according to the circumstances. 1.226.
In the act of approaching her lover, she—out of fear that her own modesty might be lost—possessed eyes like those of a fawn terrified by the roar of a tiger. (1.227)
Her body and veil were fashioned from garments dyed with indigo and other colors;
her limbs dissolved into her own form, and she moved on foot without making a sound. (1.228)
Accompanied only by her one very affectionate friend, she goes forth full of longing;
yet when her lover feigns sleep, she stands motionless at his side. (1.229)
Concealing her excessive pride with cool garlands and sandalwood paste, she, perceiving his state of mind and eager to observe his feelings, awakens him. (1.230)
For example:
"She made her ornament the same color as darkness;
she discarded the anklet because of its noisy defect."
The women going to meet their lovers did not wish to wait for the messenger girl, out of fear of the bright moonlight.
Or for example:
"Carrying garlands of jasmine, with sandalwood paste moist upon all their limbs,"
Clad in linen garments, the women going to meet their lovers are not visible in the moonlight.
(From *Kāvyādarśa* 2.213):
In the context of going to meet her lover, a maiden (*kanyakā*) should be understood as being like one's own wife (*svīyā*). 140.
(The Courtesan on Her Way to an Appointment):
The courtesan on her way to meet her lover approaches him joyful, with a face brightened by a smile and eyes rolling with intoxication. (SRs 1.234) 141
With all her limbs anointed and adorned with various ornaments,
her passion made manifest by horripilation sprouting from affection,
she was surrounded by attendants provided with the requisites for enjoyment.
The majesty of the god of love is illuminated by the sweetness of the sound of her girdle;
she is beautiful with jeweled anklets clinging to her lotus-feet,
and she delights with soft touches such as scratching his hair.
With eyes made angry out of love, she awakens him when he has fallen asleep.
Just as it is for me:
"In the month of Madhu, on a night white with moonlight, he whom a woman, afflicted by love, approaches while conversing with her friends—that man alone is truly blessed. (Śṛṅgāra-rasāṣṭaka 1.238)
Then, the woman approaching her lover had jasmine flowers from her braided hair disheveled and falling as she tossed her arms about;
her eyes were made lovely by the playfulness of moving eyebrows and other such gestures. (1.239)
Stuttering in her speech due to the intoxication of tasting liquor from which she has not desisted, the haughty woman approaches her lover together with her maidservants. 146. SRs_1.240.
For example:

"With her heavy braid of hair loosened, with playful movements of her creeper-like eyebrows, with indistinct speech arising from the intoxication of wine, and with her tender vine-like arms flung here and there at every step..."
That man alone is blessed who, having approached his beloved with longing as she lies asleep, rouses her by the tinkling sound of his jingling bracelets and then scolds her.
Now, she who, having made an appointment, is distressed because the lover does not arrive due to fate, is called "the deceived" (vipralabdha) by the wise; such is her emotional transformation. 148.
Despair, reflection, exhaustion, tears, fainting, sighing, and so forth;
as in my own [work]:
"The orb of the moon has come to the mountain of sunrise..."
"See, my friend, we have been deceived by him!
Should I take you to my own home here, or should I go there?"— thus the young bride lamented.
Now, the woman whose husband is under her own control—she whose lover is nearby and dependent on her—is called a *svādhīna-vallabhā* (one who has her beloved at her command).
Her activities are said to consist of the great festival of the worship of Smara (the God of Love). 150
Sporting in the forest, playing in the water, gathering flowers, and so forth.
As in my own [verse]:
"The playful arrangement of white lotuses in her braided hair, the trembling musk-leaf tilaka upon her cheek,"
Creating a graceful makara-design with saffron paste upon the expanse of her breasts,
that fortunate youth eternally intoxicates his beloved.
Women are all of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior.
Among them, the superior woman is she who is desired by those of noble birth, those satisfied with worldly enjoyments, and those possessed of excellent qualities.
She harbors anger only toward a cause, yet she becomes gracious when conciliated. She performs what is pleasing for her husband even while doing what is unpleasant;
even when her beloved has committed an offense, the woman of the highest class remains silent. (1.248–249)
Now, the middling woman: she desires the man herself, and she is desired by him;
when he is angry, she becomes angry repeatedly, and when he speaks falsely, she speaks falsely. (SRs_1.250) 154
She who returns harm for harm, yet feels affection for her beloved when he is kind,
and is endowed with such qualities as these, is proclaimed to be the *madhyamā* (middling) woman.
Now, the *nīcā* (low) woman—
She becomes angry without cause and does not relinquish her wrath even when entreated;
whether he be handsome or ugly, virtuous or devoid of merit, old or young—whomever she repeatedly desires. (SRs 1.252) 156. She who constantly lusts after anyone at all.
In matters of jealousy, anger, and dispute, she is known to be invariably quarrelsome (sādharmā).
The examples for these [types] are to be understood from common worldly experience alone.
Thus, the woman belonging to oneself (svīyā) is of thirteen kinds, and the excellent woman (varāṅganā) is of various types.
Thus, the courtesan (*vaiśikā*) is sixteenfold; these [sixteen] are further divided into eight stages (*avasthā*).
Each of those is eightfold according to the distinctions of "superior" (*uttama*) and so forth.
Thus, there are three hundred and eighty-four varieties.
Some say that there are only three states regarding another's wife.
For example:
A woman belonging to another may exist in three states: first, she is distressed by separation; then, having become an *abhisārikā*, she goes forth of her own accord to meet him. (SRs 1.257)
If she were to fall away from the agreement, she would be deceived once again;
for there is no other state here that is appropriate than falling into the power of another as a wife.
Thus [ends the *Bhāvaprakāśa*]. Now, the assistants of the heroine (*nāyikā-sahāya*).

Their messengers— namely the female friend, the maidservant, the female ascetic, the neighbor, the foster-sister, the artisan, the young girl, the woman skilled in weaving, the female singer, and the female fortune-teller— are endowed with the qualities of leaders and friends. (1.259–1.260)
A female ascetic (liṅginī) is one such as Paṇḍitakauśikī and others;
a neighbor (prativeśinī) is one who dwells in a house nearby;
a skilled artisan (śilpakārī) is one proficient in playing the lute and other such arts.
The *kārū* refers to washermen and the like;
the *vipraśnikā* refers to astrologers;
the remainder are well known.

Since those [rasas] that have other rasas as their objective support are not to be analyzed separately due to a lack of necessity for beginning a distinct section, we shall provide their analysis in the very context of the respective rasas themselves.
Thus ends the section on the Heroine.
Now, regarding the excitants (*uddīpana-vibhāva*) of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*):
"The excitant is fourfold, depending on its basis (*ālambana*); it is divided into qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*ceṣṭā*), ornaments (*alaṅkṛti*), and the neutral (*taṭastha*). (SRs 1.260) 162

In that regard, the qualities are as follows: youth, beauty and charm, loveliness, handsomeness, gentleness, and delicacy—these are the qualities pertaining to the objective support (ālambana). (SRs 1.261) 163
Regarding that, youth:
"The youth of all women, indeed, is fourfold; for each stage of youth, their behaviors are distinct. (SRs 1.262) 164.

Therein, [the stage of] early youth has slightly tremulous outer corners of the eyes, a lotus-face smiling with passion, cheeks with the slight ruddiness of rising pride, and lips not yet fully crimson. (SRs_1.263) 165
With limbs lovely through the emergence of grace, fragrant with the blossoming of emotion,
her breasts like sprouts just beginning to unfold, and the joints of her body still indistinct—
such was the first stage of youth in that fawn-eyed maiden.
She desires soft touch and does not tolerate excessive passion;
she delights in play with her female companions and takes care in grooming her own limbs.
She does not exhibit anger or joy upon seeing a co-wife and the like. (1.265–168)
She does not become excessively impassioned in the company of her beloved, but rather feels bashful.
Just as this expansive mass of breasts has not been brought to its natural height,
so too these three folds, radiant with lines, do not show distinct depressions or elevations.
In her center, a straight, elongated, and slightly brownish line of body hair is visible;
she abides in a lovely age that is a mixture of youth and childhood.
(This has also been cited in the *Daśarūpāvaloka*):
Her gestures are,
for example, by me [the author] himself—
The words of the Mountain’s Daughter were sweet with feigned anger, marked by the timidity of her first appearance and the disdainful yet attentive chatter of her friends.
May your efforts at this new union protect you.
Now, regarding the second stage of youth:
the breasts are full, the waist is slender, and there is a reddish hue to the hands and feet;
the thighs have the shape of an elephant’s trunk, and the limbs possess clearly defined joints.
Her hips were broad, her navel deep, and her loins firm;
the line of hair was clearly visible, and there was luster in her limbs, hair, teeth, and eyes.
By these signs, that lovely-eyed woman was known to have entered the second stage of youth.
Generally, a proud woman who knows the intentions of her friends remains affectionate toward them,
yet she does not become placated by conciliation; being envious of her co-wives,
she cannot endure their offenses when they are colored by the jealousy of her own love.
In amorous sports, she acts unrestrainedly and behaves with pride in private.
For example:
"Slender, youthful, with pointed teeth and lips like ripe bimba fruit..."
Slender at the waist, with the gaze of a startled doe, possessing a deep navel,
moving languidly from the weight of her hips, and slightly bent by her breasts—
she who exists there must be the very first creation of the Creator in the realm of young women. (Śṛṅgāra-śatakam 1.273) [Meghadūta 2.22]
Now, the third stage of youth: dryness of the eyes, a fading luster on the cheeks, a loss of radiance, a slightly rough touch to the limbs, and a slight loosening [of the body]. (SRs 1.274) 174
In the third stage of youth, the passion on the lower lip becomes smooth;
therein lies this behavior of women, their skill in the art of love: the refusal to let go of the beloved and the cleverness in attracting him. (SRs_1.275) 175.
The refusal to let go of the beloved and the skill in attracting him.
Disregard for offenses and freedom from envy even toward rival wives;
as it says in the *Ānandakośaprahasana*:
"With faces blooming through effort and cheeks marked by wrinkles..."
With their breasts, which are fleshy, heavy,
and drooping, these women surely mock even the flowers on the main road of the Lord of Love, whose stalks have loosened from their stems.

Now, regarding the fourth stage of youth—wrinkling occurs on the breasts, hips, cheeks, thighs, buttocks, and other parts; and in this fourth stage of youth, a woman also becomes fleshless. (SRs 1.278) 177
In that regard, the signs [of her affection] are: lack of enthusiasm for sexual pleasure, incapacity [for it], compliance toward rival wives, and remaining inseparable from her beloved.
As in the *Ānandakośaprahasana*: 178. For example, in the *Ānandakośaprahasana*:
With withered cheeks, sparse teeth,
sagging breasts, and conversations full of tales of the past,
and with limbs that have become slack without effort— such a woman is never to be served.
Desiring the stakes from their husbands, they have limbs languid from exhaustion.
In that regard, the suitability for the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) is the cause of aesthetic delight;
it exists only in the first and second [types of *dhvani*], not in the third and fourth.
Now, as for its form (*rūpa*):

When the limbs, though not adorned with external ornaments such as rings and the like, appear as if they were adorned by virtue of some [inherent quality], that is called *rūpa* (natural beauty). For example: 180.
Just as—
Unable to remain without her ornaments and garlands,
and longing once more to adorn her body,
a certain woman of noble form went outside.
Upon seeing her, those who were adorned with ornaments felt ashamed.
Now, regarding *lāvaṇya* (loveliness): that which appears within the limbs like the shimmering movement of a reflection within pearls is here called *lāvaṇya*. (SRs 1.284) 181.
Just as a pure and tender radiance, like reflected moonlight, expands across limbs that are as beautiful to behold as crystal mirrors. (SRs 1.285)
Now, regarding beauty:
that arrangement of the major and minor limbs which is appropriate and possesses well-knit joints is called beauty. (SRs 1.286) 182
For example: "With long eyes, a face possessing the luster of the autumnal moon, arms drooping to the shoulders, a chest with closely-set, firm, and elevated breasts, and sides as if smoothed away."
Her waist, her hips, her loins, and her feet with their curved toes—
her very body conforms to the dancer's will, just as the poetic meter conforms to the mind of the poet.
(Mālavikāgnimitra 2.3) Now, as for beauty: when, by the excellence of its own qualities, it renders another object situated nearby [insignificant].
That which leads to conformity with the wise is called "beauty" (*ābhirūpya*).
For example:
"Though this ball is but one, it appears as if it were three."
Redder than the redness of his beloved’s palm,
white as the rays from the nails of her feet upon the ground, and deep blue as the beams of her eyes while remaining in the sky— [he was seen].
Now, regarding softness (*mārdava*): that is indeed softness where a touched limb feels as if it were untouched. (Bhoja-caritra 298; SRs 1.290, 184ab)
For example: "By those two [breasts], distinguished by their fine silk garments,
the sight slips away due to their quality of smoothness."
Therefore, even at the time of creation,
there was no fear of contact with her thighs from the hands of Brahmā.
Here, even formless vision becomes slack; how much more so, then, the hands which possess form? From this description of the excellence of smoothness, softness (*mārdava*) is established.
Now, for delicacy (*saukumārya*):

That which constitutes the inability of even a delicate object to endure contact upon the limbs is *saukumārya* (delicacy); it is threefold, according to the sequence of superior, middling, and inferior. (1.292)
Now, regarding supreme delicacy (*uttama-saukumārya*): it is that by which a limb is unable to endure the touch of flowers and the like; because of this, it is "supreme. For example: [185]—
She who used to feel distressed even by the flowers from her own hair falling as she turned upon a costly bed,
now lay down resting her head upon the pillow of her vine-like arms.
"She sat down upon the bare ground alone. (SRs_1.294) [KuSaṃ 5.12].

Although the capacity to endure contact with the ground is mentioned here in the second half of the verse, it is nevertheless understood that the mind alone—fixed in its resolve—is capable of enduring affliction, and not the body; thus, her supreme delicacy is established.
Now, regarding moderate delicacy:
that limb which cannot endure the touch of a hand is indeed of moderate delicacy.
For example: [186ab]—
The very moment it was grasped by her friend’s hand, which was as tender as a young lotus,
the forefoot of a certain woman instantly turned red with lac-dye.
Furthermore, there was lac-resin, yet it did not serve as an ornament.
(The String of Pearls of Aphorisms by the Lover of Poetic Fancy [Utprekṣā-vallabha]). Now, regarding inferior delicacy:
that body which is unable to endure the heat of the sun and so forth is here considered inferior. (SRs 1.297, 186)
Just as [a lotus] imparts fragrance and delight, with its dark, clinging curls acting as bees;
In an instant, Padmā’s lotus-face became copper-hued by the soft radiance of the sun.
Their activities include *līlā*, *vilāsa*, and so forth;
these too will be discussed in the section on *anubhāvas*.
Now, for the ornament (*alaṅkṛti*):
The fourfold ornamentation consists of clothing, jewelry, garlands, and unguents. (1.299) 187ab Regarding these, as for the ornament of clothing, for example:
like the shore of the Ocean of Milk with its masses of foam...
Clad in fresh, new linen, she shone even more brightly as she held up a mirror, like an autumn night with its full moon.
The ornament of embellishment (*bhūṣālaṅkāra*), for example:
"She was like a creeper with blossoming flowers,
or like the night with rising stars."
Like a river with birds settling upon it, she shone as her ornaments were being fastened;
such was the adornment of her garlands, ointments, and jewelry. As for example: [Kuṣa-saṃhitā 7.27] Mālyānulepanālaṅkāraḥ. As for example—
The wearing of garlands upon her hair is inferred by the bees that hover there; some indescribable luster on her cheeks proclaims the betel-roll held within;
and the application of unguents is experienced through the fragrances of her limbs.
This certain clever attire of the fair-eyed woman produces pleasure for the eyes.
Then there are the indifferent things: the moonlight, the fountain-house, and the rising of the moon;
the song of the cuckoo, the mango tree, the gentle breeze, and the bees. (187)
Creeper-arbors, pavilions, underground chambers, oblong ponds, waterfalls,
188 palaces, inner sanctuaries, music halls, pleasure-mountains, rivers, and so forth—
these should be conceived accordingly as being suitable for enjoyment at the appropriate time. 189
In that context, the moonlight serves as an excitant (uddīpana), as in:
"In the bower of creepers, difficult to approach because of the moonlight, Lalitā was hidden by her circle of friends."
Having seen somewhere a drop of moonlight fallen from the beak of a *cakora* bird, she fell into a swoon.
Of the fountain-house: for instance,
she was unable even to stand upon the moonstone pedestal, though it was made of moonstones.
Having reached that fountain-house, she considered it to be the house of the terrible sword-edge of the bodiless god of love.
As in the case of the rising moon: "Look, O friend, the orb of the moon has come to the mountain of sunrise; by that we have been deceived."
At this, the bride was distressed, wondering: "Should I take me to my own home, or should I stay here?"
Regarding the song of the cuckoo, for example: "The male cuckoo, its throat made harsh by tasting the sprouts of the mango tree, uttered its sweet cry."

That very speech of Smara has become skilled in shattering the pride of the high-minded woman, as in the *Mākandasya* (verse 3.32): *manasvinī-māna-vighāta-dakṣaṃ tad eva jātaṃ vacanaṃ smarasya //* [Kuṣaṇḍikā 3.32] *mākandasya*, as follows—
This young mango tree, long cherished with sprinklings of water from jars held in one's own hands,
now produces the arrows of the Flower-Armed God.
This very [milk] is that which nourishes the serpent with its fluid.
"Mākanda" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for the Aśoka tree and others;
[it refers to] the gentle breeze, as in:
"It was deeply drunk in by the women of the serpent-king."
It emerged along with that poison;
otherwise, how could the southern wind, being itself powerless, have destroyed her?
Of the humming of six-legged bees, as if with unprecedented mantras of sweet sounds, languid with intoxication.
The glories of spring perform the exorcism of the pride of women who are possessed by resentment.
Of the vine-arbor, as follows:
this grove of betel-nut trees has blossoming flowers and mango trees at its borders; in its center is a lake with a gentle breeze that brings bliss to the end of amorous dalliance.
On its bank stands a graceful plantain bower; within it is a pavilion of jasmine creepers, where that fair-eyed woman watches the path for you.
Of the underground chamber— for example,
in underground chambers perfumed by the fragrance of the rising smoke of black aloe-wood incense.
There, men did not suffer from the cold winds of the month of Māgha, for they took refuge in the warmth of the breasts of dark-complexioned women.
In the long pond, for instance—
where the great stalks of white lotuses quiver, shaken by the wings of mallikākṣa geese warbling with intoxication.
Let the regions of the eyes, possessing uninterrupted beauty in the interval between the falling and rising of the water of tears, be beheld.
(From *Mālatīmādhava* 9.14) Regarding the power of the clouds, as it is said:
"The mind of high-minded women is even more fickle than the mind of the god of love."
Thus dispelled by the roar of the clouds,
even those who were skilled and renowned for their transgressions became,
for a moment, as if angry when embraced.
In this context, the mention of "clouds and wood" is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of lightning and so forth;
for example, as lightning flashes with momentary brilliance during those rains.
The cowherd woman embraced Mādhava;
and that lightning, having beheld the splendor of his limbs,
entered the cloud quickly as if out of shame.
As in the interior of a palace, where peacocks perch upon the rafters and pigeons dwell in the pigeon-cotes;
He took delight, second only to the aesthetic sentiment (rasa), within the inner chambers of the palaces, which were difficult to traverse even for the winds from the clouds.
As an example of *saṅgīta* (conjoined):
"Mādhava [was] in a bower of sweet mādhavī vines, where bees were buzzing loudly."
He sang with his flute, which was charming to the ear and served as a hook for the fish of the pride of the gopīs.
From the Play-Mountain (Krīḍādri), as follows:
"You should dwell upon the mountain named Nīca there for the sake of rest;
through contact with you, it seems to thrill, as it were, with its full-blown *kadamba* flowers."
It is that which proclaims the unrestrained youth of the city-dwellers through its stone mansions, from which waft the fragrances of dalliance with virtuous women.
As for the rivers: [as in Meghadūta 1.26]—
Then, on the Sarayū river— where rows of waves were like intoxicated royal swans and which bore the flowers of the creepers along its banks— the King, accompanied by his wife, desired to sport.
"In the water, which was pleasant in the summer, he stayed" (Ra.vam.
16.54); other examples such as this should also be cited.
Now, the *anubhāvas* (consequents):
Those gestures and manifestations directed toward an object which directly reveal the internal state of mind— that is, their own cause—
are known as *anubhāvas*, such as the raising of the eyebrows, smiles, and so forth. (SRs 1.321) 190
These arise from fourfold undertakings of mind, body, speech, and intellect;
therein are *bhāva*, *hāva*, *helā*, *śobhā*, *kānti*, and *dīpti*.
*Prāgalbhya* (boldness), *mādhurya* (sweetness), *dhairya* (fortitude), and *audārya* (noble-mindedness) are the states born of the mind.

In this context, *hāva* is the slight manifestation of mental modifications— such as anger, joy, or shame— through means such as sidelong glances, smiles, or downcast faces. Now, *helā* is that which is clearly expressed through various transformations indicative of the form of amorous passion (*śṛṅgāra*).
*Hela* is indeed *hāva* itself, consisting of graceful gestures (*lalitābhinaya*).
For example:
"Revealing her emotion through her limbs, the Daughter of the Mountain... [SRs 1.328] (194)
With her face turned slightly to the side, her eyes cast downward, and her countenance as lovely as a blossoming young kadamba flower, she stood there.
In this context, *helā* (sportiveness) consists in the extreme manifestation of mental activity through transformations such as horripilation, turning the face aside, and rolling the eyes.
Regarding that, *śobhā* (beauty):
it is the adornment of the limbs that arises from beauty, enjoyments, and so forth. (SRs 1.330, 195ab)
For example:
"Because of the tight embrace, the body-unguents remained half-applied; because the force of passion did not cease, her braid hung down from her shoulder."
We worship Uṣas, who, rising from her bedchamber, stumbles with the hem of her garment held in her palm, her eyes full of timidity.
Now, *kānti* (loveliness): Luster itself is declared to be *kānti*, radiant with the nourishment of the god of love. For example: [195cd]—*śobhaiva kāntir ākhyātā manmathāpyāyanojjvalā*.
As for example: [text follows].

As she rises at the end of love-making, supporting the weight upon the lord of serpents with one hand and holding her garment with the other while bearing the burden of her loosened tresses upon her shoulder—
may Śauri, his joy of union redoubled by her beauty at that moment, protect you.
May the body of Lakṣmī, its arms languidly yet gracefully raised as she embraces her bed, purify you.

(Veṇīsaṃhāra 1.3) Here, because the beauty of the body produced by a previous sexual union serves as the cause for the commencement of a subsequent one, it possesses the quality of nourishing the god of love (*manmatha*).
Now, [the quality of] *dīpti* (brilliance):
When *kānti* (loveliness) itself reaches an extreme expansion through the qualities of age, enjoyment, place, time, and so forth, it is called *dīpti* (brilliance). For example: [196]—

There, at midnight, when your obstruction has ceased and the moonbeams are clear, the cobwebs hanging from the limbs of women— limbs exhausted by the embrace of their lovers' arms after lovemaking— [are illuminated].
The moonstones, dripping with clear drops of water, cause [the travelers] to falter.

SRs_1.335 // [Meghadūta 2.9] Here, through qualities such as the embrace of the beloved, the moonlight on the palace roof, and so forth, a brilliance (*dīpti*) consisting of the enthusiasm for further sexual union is perceived, because it dispels the exhaustion resulting from lovemaking. Now, audacity (*prāgalbhya*):
Freedom from hesitation in practical applications is proclaimed as "boldness" (prāgalbhya).
[This was attained] by her who, in secret, sought refuge with Śaṅkara, the teacher of the arts of love, while she was still a student.
The very skill in youth that she had learned was offered as a teacher’s fee (*guru-dakṣiṇī-kṛta*).
Here, by the expression "offered as a teacher’s fee," her boldness in the form of retaliation is conveyed.
Now, sweetness (*mādhurya*):
sweetness is the gentleness of gestures in all circumstances. For example: [197cd]—*SRs_1.338*—as follows:

she cast her gaze toward the mosaic floor where flowers were being tossed about by her big toe.
From her dancing, the half [of her body] that remained standing was exceedingly beautiful and straight-extended.
In this passage from the *Mālavikāgnimitra* (2.6),
the actions such as the plucking of flowers with the big toe possess sweetness (*mādhurya*) because of their beauty (*cārutva*), even though they occur at the conclusion of a dance performance.

As found in the *Ujjvala-nīlamaṇi*,
the word used here in place of *mārdava* is [the following]. Now, regarding fortitude (*dhairya*):

(Māgha 13.16) The term "meeting with friends" (*mitra-saṅgama*) is also an elliptical expression for meeting with those worthy of honor and so forth. For example, by means of meeting with those worthy of honor—
The worlds, which rested in full expansion within his body when he had withdrawn himself at the time of the end of the eon,
could not be contained therein by the enemy of Kaṭabha.
Joys arise from the attainment of the wealth of asceticism;
through divine favor,
as [in the case] of her whose face was like the bright moon, [he granted] grace.
Having reported [the matter] to his preceptor,
he then announced it to his beloved by means of words that were like a redundancy, as it had already been inferred from the signs of her great joy. (RaVaṃ 2.68)
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), [factors] such as the grace of the king of gurus are included.
Through the grace of the guru, for example:
"Today this sun, the foremost among those who enjoy the sacrificial offerings, has arisen as the great-grandfather of our lineage."
"We are sacrificers today; O Blessed Earth, today you possess a king.
Today Indra considers himself fortunate because of us, his companions, since even the husband of Arundhatī bestows such grace upon us. (Raghuvamśa 1.18)
Through the king's favor, just as his pleasure increased as he gave, so too did the kings who desired to do what was pleasing to him [increase].
They experienced even greater joy from the gifts being touched than from those placed within the house;
now, [there follows] the eagerness (autsukya).
Impatience with time is longing arising from separation from a desired object;

its activities include the desire to see that object or other beautiful things, as well as restlessness, lack of stability, lying on one's back in bed while reflecting, and so forth. (SRs 2.177) 81. Restlessness, lack of stability, and lying on one's back while reflecting.
Heaviness of the body, sleep, lethargy, sighing, and so forth [occur].
In that state, due to separation from a beloved object,
how can the three watches of the night— though long— be contracted as if they were a single moment?
In every state, how could even the day have such faint heat?
Thus, O lady of tremulous eyes, my heart— its prayers difficult to fulfill—
is rendered helpless by the intense fevers of the agony of separation from you.

There, when her beloved had arrived from seeing her desired object, she spent the day somehow with hundreds of longings; then, as the dull-witted attendants went to the bedchamber and were engaged in a lengthy conversation, the slender-limbed woman, saying "I have been bitten! quickly shook off her silken garment and, with a mind anxious for union, extinguished the lamp. (Amaru 77)
Out of a desire to see what was beautiful, with the remainder of what had been done, with graceful movements, and having filled the path by unfastening [the garment].
To behold Acyuta, the women of the city resorted to the windows after having adorned themselves.

Now, (27) ferocity (*augrya*) is the state of being fierce (*ugratā*), consisting of cruelty produced by chasing after those who have committed offenses, by seizing them for theft and so forth, and by means of false accusations and the like. (SRs 2.181) 83.
In that regard, his actions include redness of the eyes, binding, and flogging;
shaking the head, as well as expressions of exhaustion, beating, and threats, [arising] from an offense, for example: [SRs_2.182] 84. From an offense, as follows—

Upon that body which grows weary even from being struck by playful blossoms of the *śirīṣa* tree— blossoms obtained through the savor of affectionate jests with her loving friend— if you were to hurl a weapon for the purpose of slaying it, [you would incur great sin].
"Let this arm of Śara fall like a sudden, unprovoked bolt of lightning.
(Mālatīmādhava 5.31). Here, Mādhava’s ferocity arises from the offense consisting of the insult to Mālatī.
As for [ferocity] arising from humiliation:
His mind enraged by the previously unknown contempt shown by his enemies, he—
whose actions were censured even by the wise— addressed the messenger of the command.
Yajñāśivi’s enemy struck him with a mace.
Because of being caught in the act of theft—for example:
"Fie upon you! You who, out of pride in your vine-like arms, were blinded by your own vanity, now flee while being reviled with the cry of 'Thief!'"
"May Jaṭāyu, whose cruel deeds are performed with the tips of his curved claws, perform his own act of defecation upon your breast! (A.Rā. 5.11).
An example of frivolous talk (*asat-pralāpa*) is as follows:

For some reason, my father Drupada—though pained and fearful—did not forbid it; yet today, as you boast of the pride of your arm's strength, this left foot of mine is being placed upon your head. Ward him off!
(Veṇīsaṃhāra 3.40) Now, (28) indignation (*amarṣa*): Indignation is said to be anger [arising] from insults, humiliation, and the like.
In that state, there is perspiration, trembling of the head, downward-looking, and reflection;
the activities consist of seeking means, enthusiasm, and exertion. (2.187)
In that regard, by way of reproach, for example:
"As if they had suddenly understood the meaning of the words spoken by Bhīṣma..."
Then the host of kings on the side of Śiśupāla fell into extreme agitation due to that insult, as follows: (Śiśupālavadha 15.47). Due to the insult—
If indignation does not provide me, who am immediately overwhelmed by enemies, with the support of my arms for retaliation, then my heart is surely destroyed. (Ki.
11.57) Now, [the section on] envy (asūyā):
Envy (*asūyā*) is the attribution of faults even where virtues exist, caused by another's excellence in fortune, wealth, learning, valor, and so forth.
Its manifestations include turning away the face, reproach, knitting the eyebrows, and showing disregard. (SRs 2.190–191)
By means of another's good fortune, as for example:
"Do not harbor pride, thinking, 'The cluster of blossoms written by my beloved’s own hand shines upon the surface of my cheek.'"
O friend, why should any other woman not also be a fit vessel for such things, provided that trembling— the enemy— does not stand as an obstacle within?
(Regarding Keśaṭa, in the *Subhāṣitaratnakośa*):
Through the prosperity of others— just as wealth that benefits the world belongs to the virtuous whose minds are stainless.
Nevertheless, upon merely beholding her, those of wicked mind are tormented.

If the Vedāntas, by means of false knowledge, propound matters contradicted by what is established through the light of perception and other means of valid cognition, then what wrong have the Buddhists done? (SRs 2.193; Pra.ca. 2.4)
Or as it is said:
"O Lion among Kings, while your fame— residing in a vessel of virtues— shines forth in fullness, and while your majesty consumes your enemies,"
"Aha! The sage Kaṇāda, whose intellect is most deluded, has declared that there are only nine substances, even though he divided fire itself into four types. (SRs 2.194)

Here, through the commencement of speech— characterized by great envy toward Kaṇāda, who propounds the doctrine of limited substances, on the part of a speaker who follows the path well-established in the tradition of mature poets— it is manifested that his intellect is most dull, just as [the heroism of another is revealed] by the valor of a foe:
"Tāṭakā was indeed merely a woman, while Rāma, the son of Bhṛgu, is a pure Brahmin."
Mārīca was merely a deer, a source of fear; Vālī, moreover, was but a monkey.
O descendant of Kakutstha, why do you boast? Or rather, what hero have you conquered?
Nevertheless, if such is your pride in your arms, then string your bow in my presence.
(Hanumannāṭaka 14.21) Now, regarding fickleness: Fickleness is the lightness of the mind caused by passion, hatred, and so forth.
In that state, there are actions such as embracing and clinging without deliberation, as well as harsh words of expulsion, striking, and ordering about. (2.196)
Out of passion— for instance,
having forcibly seized him thinking "it is deserted," and then seeing another woman, his rival, nearby for a moment—
Desirous of flying up out of fear of her own lightness, she became exceedingly heavy when her beloved let go of her. (Śiśupālavadha 7.57)
— as in the case of hatred:
O Malaya breezes, quickly strike Surabhi on all sides with kicks of your feet; O chains, provide a heavy bond of fragrance!
Cast the King of Ragas, Pañcama, swiftly into prison.
Grind the moon into powder upon a stone slab, and grind the reflected image into dust.

In this passage from the *Bālarāmāyaṇa* (5.49), Rāvaṇa’s restlessness (*cāpalya*) is illuminated by his aversion toward objects such as spring due to his separation from Sītā, and by the consequent gestures of striking and commanding the presiding deities of those seasons.
Now, (31) sleep (*nidrā*).

Sleep is the closing of the mind caused by intoxication, natural disposition, physical exertion, lack of anxiety, fatigue, and so forth; its characteristic signs therein are heaviness of the face and [the body]. (89) SRs_2.199//
Rolling of the eyes, rubbing of the limbs,
frequent sighing and gasping, drooping of the body, closing of the eyes, contraction of the frame, and numbness— these and other such symptoms [occur]. (SRs 2.200–201)
Out of intoxication, as for example:
"When he praises the earth, sleep departs from the women who have reached the halfway point on their way to the pleasure gardens."
Even the wind did not dishevel her garments;
who would have ventured to stretch out a hand to seize them?
This is by her very nature, as for example: [RaVaṃ 6.75] svabhāvāt, yathā—
Having laid down one creeper-like arm supine upon her broad expanse of hips, and resting the other languidly against the corner of her eye,
she loosened her girdle slightly as she let out a deep sigh.
The slender-waisted woman sleeps with her breasts pressed against the bed and tilted sideways.
From physical exertion— for example:
[the breasts] which have been massaged by loose embraces following the fatigue produced by the journey of another woman, languid and charming from weariness.

Where, having placed upon my chest your limbs as frail as crushed lotus stalks, you obtained sleep; because of your state of carefree ease, as it were— (Uttara-rāma-carita 1.24) —just as: [text continues]
By your profound conduct— which possesses a multitude of arms wondrously manifesting the grace of granting fearlessness— Nārāyaṇa has been rendered slack in his efforts to protect the three worlds,
[his own] vital breath being filled by the wind of your exhalations, which consist of the cool fragrance of internal satisfaction.
Now, on a couch of serpents raised high by his vital breath, he sleeps peacefully from exhaustion, out of mere compassion for his beloved. (A.Rā. 1.27) As, for example:
"Merely out of kindness toward his beloved..."
As the rows of luminaries bent down, he, whose chest was embraced by them, felt a longing to close his eyes. (Kuṣa-saṃhitā 8.84)
Now, (32) sleep: Sleep is indeed the excess of *nidrā*; therein the modifications (*vikriyā*) are the cessation of the sense organs, the closing of the eyes, and the drooping of the limbs. 92
Furthermore, there are also excessive dreaming, restlessness, labored inhalation and exhalation, and so forth.
Just as she whose heart is moistened by the essence of compassion,
from whom the fragrance of the Upanishads naturally emanates—
The breath-winds of Murāri as he sleeps shall be the remnants of what has been drunk by the king of serpents upon his couch.

Now, (33) awakening: through dreaming, touch, sound, sleep, fullness, and so forth, there is awakening; it is the attainment of consciousness, and its activities therein include the rubbing of the eyes. (SRs 2.208)
Leaving the bed, tossing the arms, cracking the fingers, scratching the head, twisting the limbs, and so forth—these are [the faults]. (2.209)
From sleep— for instance,
when three parts of the night remained, he closed his eyes for a moment and suddenly woke up.
"O blue-throated one, where are you going?"— thus she spoke with an indistinct voice,
her arms bound around his neck in a false embrace.
(Kuṣa-saṃhitā 5.57) As for [the power] from touch:
Having smelled the face of the long-eyed woman at her lower lip—
she who was then asleep from the exhaustion of hurried dalliance— he thought, "This is the morning breeze, fragrant with the scent of lotuses."
Having come to the jeweled window, he awakened me.
From sound, for example:
"At dawn, he was awakened from sleep by the flapping of the ears of the elephant herd, which sounded like the sharp beat of kettledrums."
There he took delight while listening to the sweet warbling of birds and the auspicious songs of bards;
through the fulfillment of his sleep, as follows—
They reached the ocean, and the Primeval Person (Ādi-puruṣa) became aware of it;
for lack of distraction is indeed the sign of the accomplishment of a future task.
(Ra-vam 10.6) Among the superior, inferior, and middling types, the sattvic [emotions] are the transitory states (vyabhicārin). 95.
They should be described as appropriate through the transitory (vibhāva) and consequent (anubhāva) states.
(2.214) Mental fluctuations such as agitation, affection, hypocrisy, and envy are included within those already mentioned; therefore, they are not shown separately. (2.215)
[*13] The editor adds: The mental states not explicitly mentioned are included within those that have been stated.

For instance, *dambha* (deceit), which consists in the form of cheating others, is included within *jihmā* (crookedness) and *avahitthā* (concealment). *Sneha* (affection), characterized by the melting of the heart, is included within *harṣa* (joy).

Envy (*īrṣyā*), which consists of intolerance toward the giving of gifts or honors by one's own objects [of affection], is included within intolerance (*amarṣa*); whereas envy directed toward the objects of others is included within malice (*asūyā*).
Furthermore, agitation (*udvega*) should be understood as being included, as appropriate, within despondency (*nirveda*), dejection (*viṣāda*), and so forth. Thus it should be seen.
And so says the author of the Bhāvaprakāśikā:
"If other mental states (bhāvas) should also exist as particular modifications of the mind, they must all be seen as included among the transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāvas). (SRs 2.216)
The *vibhāvas* (determinants) and *anubhāvas* (consequents) exist in relation to one another; their relationship as cause and effect is generally to be understood from worldly experience. (2.217)

For instance: distress (*santāpa*) is a determinant cause (*vibhāva*) with respect to dejection (*dainya*) and an ensuant effect (*anubhāva*) with respect to exhaustion (*glāni*). A blow (*prahāra*) is a determinant cause with respect to paralysis and delusion (*pralaya-moha*) and an ensuant effect with respect to ferocity (*augrya*).
Despair (*viṣāda*) is an ensuant effect with respect to the onset of calamity (*utpātāvega*) and a determinant cause with respect to paralysis (*stambha*).
Disease functions as a determinant cause (*vibhāva*) with respect to languor, paralysis, fainting, and so forth.
These transitory mental states (*vyabhicārin*) are of two kinds: independent and dependent.
Those that have attained the status of nourishing another [emotion] are called "dependent. (98)
And it is taught that in the absence of that [dependence], entities would be independent:
"In that regard, there is disenchantment with dependence, as follows:
'If these sprouts of humanity in the lineage of Manu were to engage in talk of weapons...'"

If this group of Brahmins is considered by you to be a group of mere figures, and if you hold that the most effective means for kings and sacrificial fuel-sticks is the act of cutting, then fie on this hand of mine, scarred with prominent knots from the friction of drawing the bowstring and kusha grass! (A.Rā. 4.44)
In this instance, there is the subordination of despondency (*nirveda*) to anger (*krodha*).
As for the independence of despondency, it is as follows:
"Wealth that milks all desires has been obtained; what of it?"
What is gained by placing one's foot upon the heads of enemies?
What is gained by providing wealth to those who seek favor?
What is gained by bodies of embodied beings that endure for an entire kalpa? (SRs 2.220) [Vaiśeṣika-śataka 67]
And so forth. Here, because dispassion (*nirveda*) is not a subordinate limb [of another rasa], it possesses independence.
Now, if it is asked: "Since some have stated that dispassion is the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of the *śānta* (peaceful) rasa, how can it serve as an accessory to other rasas?"—it is replied:
Indeed, when there is a village, there is the possibility of a boundary.

What is called "stability" is the repeated renewal of a state— which exists in the form of a latent impression (*vāsanā*)— through the proficiency of mental formations (*saṃskāra*), [and] which is awakened by the force of causes.

Therefore, since it is impossible for spectators to engage with the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth at the outset— because they are regarded as fruitless— the very arising of *nirveda* (disgust), which is the result of that causal complex, cannot be logically established within the minds of spectators already permeated by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of *nirveda*.
How much less, then, could there be its status as a permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*)?

Furthermore, if there were no *nirveda* (disgust) as its underlying stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*), the aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*) of the *śānta* (quiescent) rasa for spectators would be like the discernment of royal parrots who are greedy for the taste of plantain fruit depicted in a painting;
thus, enough of this agitation.
As for the dependence of despondency (*viṣāda*), it is as follows:
Again and again, a flood of tears rises up and veils my vision;
my body reaches a state of numbness and rigidity brought about by the constant brooding upon him.
"This hand of mine, immediately perspiring with fingers incessantly trembling and wavering, is utterly occupied with the task of drawing lines; what am I to do? (Mālatīmādhava 1.38).
Here, despondency serves as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*).
Independence, for example:
"Like the flickering flame of a lamp at night, that maiden choosing her own husband passed by whomever she encountered."
"That protector of the earth fell into a state of pallor like a turret on the road of a king"—
in this instance, despondency is not subordinate to any other element.

In this way, the independence or dependence of other [factors] should also be inferred in their respective places. These [factors] would possess the nature of a mere appearance because they proceed from what is improper;
and because of being unreal and because of being unfitting, this "impropriety" (anaucitya) is twofold. (100)
That which pertains to insentient things would be caused by unreality.
For example:
"Who are you, sir?
"Know me to be a wretched fate, a śākhoṭaka tree; you speak as if out of world-weariness."
Well understood! Why is this being said?
Here, the traveler serves that banyan tree with his whole soul, yet not even its shade performs a service for others, even though it stands upon the path. (SRs 2.224)

In this case, because it is a specific type of tree, and since a modification of the mind is impossible in an insentient *śākhoṭaka* tree, this inappropriate despondency attains the status of a semblance (*ābhāsa*). That which is produced by unfitness is said to have its locus in base beings, animals, or humans. (SRs 2.225) 101. Among these, that which pertains to base beings and animals is as follows:
Give birth upon the shore; do not be apprehensive in your mind.
This ocean knows me, the ṭiṭṭibha, who am fond of daring exploits. (SRs 2.226)

In this regard, when his own wife becomes apprehensive— thinking that if she were to give birth at the seashore, her offspring might be carried away by the garlands of overflowing waves— a certain *ṭiṭṭibha*, a specific species of bird,
prides himself [on his ability to prevent this].
This pride, however, being characteristic of a base animal, is merely a semblance (*ābhāsa*) and does not taste very sweet.

Resorting to base men is like this: [a man] who is prone to sleeping on his back, with the beauty of a pillow provided by his own pair of hands, [rests] at the foot of a *gandhūraka* tree, accompanied by the sounds echoing from his hollowed knees.
First, that mean man, exhausted by his labors in the field, falls asleep with his two lips bitten and emitting hundreds of hisses through long, heavy breaths.
The four stages of the transitory emotions (*vyabhicārin*) are origination, union, mixture, and subsidence. Among these, "origination" (*utpatti*) is the emergence of a state (*bhāva*).
For example: [102] Just as—

While the celestial sage was speaking thus, Pārvatī, standing at her father’s side with her face cast downward, began counting the petals of her play-lotus. Herein, there is the emergence of either shame or joy.

If two entities—whether similar or dissimilar, and conceived through distinct causes—come together, that is called *sandhi* (juxtaposition). An example of the *sandhi* of two intrinsic natures (*svarūpa*) is as follows: [text omitted].
Of those who had fallen to the earth by the blows of lions and rhinoceroses— the ships for the noble ones—
and whose limbs were cast upon the laps of their beloveds;
There occur the closing of the corners of the eyes.
Here, the conjunction (*sandhi*) of the delusions produced in the rival leaders by both the hero’s sword-stroke and the touch of his beloved’s limbs is manifested through the closing of their eyes;
this is a conjunction of dissimilar elements (*asarūpa-sandhi*), as seen in the case of the rival leaders of King Śrī Siṃha.
Their limbs perspire and tremble excessively amidst the thundering sounds that resonate with musical instruments,
while their necks are embraced by their beloveds.

Here, in the midst of the roars, there is a *sandhi* (junction), conceived as a union through the similarity between sweat and trembling, of the fear that has sprouted in the antagonists due to the suspicion that the hero’s armor is being polished, and of the joy rippling from the embrace of their beloveds.
The dissolution of an emotion that has reached its peak is called *śānti* (subsidence). [SRK 2.233, 104ab]
Just as [the sprout] within the inner apartments,
though warded off by conciliatory gestures, grew fearlessly;
and though checked by the words of advice from aged ministers, it continued to increase.
The tree of the excessive pride of rival kings is uprooted from its very foundation even when the army of King Anapotasiṃha is merely sighted.

Here, by means of the verbal expression, the pacification of the pride residing in the antagonist—which had arisen from a disregard for salutary advice—is shown to be uprooted from its very foundation. However, "complexity" (*śabalatva*) would be the mutual intermingling of emotional states (*bhāva*), as in:
104. For example:

Who indeed shall conquer us, the ornaments of the Lunar dynasty, on the field of battle? Fie upon our arms! That cursed Fate has struck us down; why then do we take refuge in a fortress, when he has already slain our ancestral kings who were long-lived?
What is the use of words for King Anapotasiṃha? Service alone is his supreme duty.
In this context, the convergence of pride, despondency, envy, anxiety, memory, resentment, world-weariness, and intelligence is called *bhāva-śabalatvam* (the commingling of emotions).
Thus, all the transitory states (*sañcārin*), along with their elaborations, have been described by King Siṃha, whose fame travels through the intermediate quarters of the sky. (SRs 2.237) 105.
Thus end the transitory emotions (sañcāribhāvas). Now, as for the stable emotions (sthāyins):
those which are not overwhelmed by emotions of their own kind or of a different kind [are the stable emotions].
For those stable emotions lead others, like rivers flowing into the ocean, to become one with their own nature.
Bharata has described these as love, laughter, energy, wonder, anger, sorrow, disgust, and fear; thus there are eight, and their characteristics will now be explained.
In that regard, passion (*rati*) is defined as follows: "Passion is the enduring desire between two young people directed toward one another;
it arises through nature, through application, through association, and through self-conceit. (SRs 2.240) 108.
In that context, this transformation (*vikriyā*) may arise through internal objects of comparison;
it is considered to consist of side-long glances, the raising of eyebrows, affectionate speech, and so forth.
(SRs 2.241) 109. In that regard, natural passion (*rati*) is as follows:
Enough with this dispute; let him remain exactly as you have heard him to be in every respect.
My mind, however, remains fixed here on the singular essence of my devotion.
One engaged in sensual desire does not perceive what ought to be said.

(Kuṣa-saṃ 5.82) Here, Pārvatī’s passion, which is independent of perceived causes such as beauty and the like, arises from her very nature (*nisarga*) in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from a previous birth.
"Application" (*abhiyoga*) means intense attachment (*abhiniveśa*).
That is to say, the state of being solely intent upon that;
by means of which [state], as it were, my mind is distracted by that charming blow.
Beholding me, her upper garment slipping unnoticed and her eyes darting like those of a frightened yearling fawn, she embraced me with limbs as if steeped in nectar. (Mālatīmādhava 4.8)
In this case, Makaranda’s love for her arises through association, indicated by such things as the slipping of his upper garment, which reveals Madayantika’s passionate advances; just as it is said:
"The king was born from a place of sacrifice to the gods, and his father was a teacher of the Veda."
Her form, exceedingly serene and radiant, inspires affection in me. (SRs 2.244; MaVīCa 1.21).
Here, Rāma’s love for Sītā arises from the weight of their relationship as a deity, a sacrificer, and a father-in-law. Now, [the next topic is] pride (*abhimāna*).

Abhimāna is the intention that "this alone is dear to me, and nothing else. By means of that [abhimāna], as it is said: "In this world, there are various victorious entities—such as the crescent of the new moon and others—which are naturally sweet and which indeed intoxicate the mind."
"But for me, that she—who is the moonlight for my eyes—has come within the range of my vision is the sole great festival of this life. (Mālatīmādhava 1.39).

Here, through Mādhava’s self-identification with her as the "moonlight for his eyes" and the "great festival for his vision," and through his lack of desire for any other lovely object, there is *rati* (love/attachment) toward Mālatī.
By way of analogy: just as he did not take as his arrow's mark the peacock flying up from near the horse with its beautiful plumage.
"Instantly his mind went to the tresses of his beloved, which were strewn with variegated garlands and whose binding had loosened during their amorous play. (Ra.Vaṃ.
9.67) Here, although King Daśaratha’s passion for his beloved was interrupted by the hunt, that passion is reawakened by the sight of a peacock’s plumage resembling her mass of hair.

Internally, there is only the authority of my own self; therefore, as I wish, I remember that I did not accept the daughters of the Sage when they were offered. Yet, my heart, though it be so, seems to convince me that it is deeply pained. (Śakuntalā 5.31)
Here, Duṣyanta’s passion for Śakuntalā persists even though she has forgotten the curse due to the evidence of his own mental anguish;
the objects [of sense] are sound and so forth,
among which, by means of sound—
As it has been said by me:
"O friend, for me, who am struck down by destiny, let there be a sight of him or let there not be."
Furthermore, if that sound of the flute should fall upon the path of one's ears, that alone is sufficient.
In this case, even though Kṛṣṇa had not been seen before, there was an arousal of passion in the Kāmavallī by the sound of his flute and by his touch, as in: "When,
due to the jolting of the chariot, the shoulder of this fair-hipped woman [touched] shoulder to shoulder..."
Touched by his form, she experienced a thrill of horripilation as if love had sprouted within her.
As for his appearance:
"This is Rāma; this is not he who shattered the sacrificial post of Janaka."
"This is not Kāma; this one, however, has a mind intoxicated by the pride of honey-wine.
O friend, it is known: he is that very King Siṃha, who is the fruit produced by the eyes of young women and the source of all fortunes; he truly triumphs! (SRs 2.250)
In this case, the love of a certain woman arises through the excellence of the hero's form, which serves as the cause for her remembrance of Rāma and others;
[this occurs] by means of rasa, as in:
"But Hara, his composure slightly impaired..."
Like the ocean at the onset of the rising moon, he fixed his eyes upon Umā’s face, where the lower lip was like the fruit of the *bimba*. (Kuṣa-saṃ. 3.67)
In this context, although it may seem inconsistent for the lower lip— which was previously unknown as a *vibhāva* for the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) prior to the act of tasting—
to function as such a *vibhāva*, nevertheless, the status of the well-known and expected flavor itself as a *vibhāva* is suggested by the phrase "the bimba-fruit-like lower lip.
Alternatively, the Supreme Lord, having tasted the bimba-fruit-like lower lip of Dākṣāyaṇī, experiences love for her even when she is encountered in another birth, solely through that same flavor.
