Having begun thus and ending with "The ocean is the seventh incarnation of Vaikuṇṭha" (prior to verse 7.44), the *saṅgraha* (synopsis) is established by the collection of the mutual affectionate words between the ocean and Rāmacandra; now follows the *anumāna* (inference).
The inference of a matter from a sign is called *anumāna*.
For example, in that same work (*Bālarāmāyaṇa*, 7.21,
preceding the verse), the female doorkeeper (looking all around):
"How is it that this ocean appears as if it were something else?
Vandī (observing with wonder in the direction previously indicated): "Look!
Beginning with the sight of pairs of *mānuṣas* dissolving in the water and the herds of female conches being excessively tormented..."
The female doorkeeper:
Yes, it is known; in the city of Vārāṇasī, flaming arrows fall from the Lord of the Raghus.
By this [passage] ending with "ity antena," there is *anumāna* (inference), because it describes the purpose of Rāma’s resolve as inferred from the signs of the ocean's agitation.
Now, the *toṭaka*:
they indeed declare that speech accompanied by fury is *toṭaka*. (SRs 3.113, 56a)
Just as in that very *Bālarāmāyaṇa*, Hanumān says: "As my master commands" (looking all around)—
"let the monkey warriors, who sport with arrogant prowess, listen to the son of Sugrīva."
With palms joined at your crowns, having received our command for this arrangement,
go forth to all the quarters; what indeed is difficult for you to accomplish in bringing here the mountains uprooted from their foundations by the striking of your two staff-like arms?
Thus, beginning from this point and continuing until the conclusion of the act, because of the description of the agitation caused by the monkeys, rākṣasas, and others, it is *toṭaka*.
Now, regarding *adhibala*:
"The wise have declared *adhibala* to be excessive deception through guile. (SRs 3.115, 56b)
As it is said in that very work, the *Bālarāmāyaṇa*, in the sixth act (prior to verse 6.5): Māyāmaya says— “Now once,
while Daśaratha, whose desires of his friends were fulfilled, was together with Kaikeyī— who was full of affection for her beloved— setting out for victory over the hosts of asuras, and while Indra,
the ornament of heaven, had arrived in his powerful form, [Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa] assumed his appearance.”

Having begun with, "Śūrpaṇakhā and I arrived at Ayodhyā to deceive Rāma, who is as delightful as a blue lotus, along with his retinue," Mālyavān concludes with, "What is impossible for cleverness? (after verse 6.5), describing how the illusory Śūrpaṇakhā and he themselves deceived Rāma and Vāmadeva by assuming deceptive disguises.
Regarding superior force:
now, as for agitation (*udvega*), fear arising from enemies, enmity, and so forth is called agitation. (SRs 3.116, 57a)
Just as in that same place [prior to verse 6.56]: (Then enters Ratnaśikhaṇḍa, with a mime of descending from the middle of the sky)—"Hail to the great king Daśaratha!
Daśaratha: "Is it well with my friend Jaṭāyu?"
Ratnaśikhaṇḍa: "By means of my dear friend's service, and not by my own body. Daśaratha: "My good man, sit down and speak."
Having begun with "I am distraught," she says: "O God! You have brought about this mockery for the Rāghava family, who have gone to the forest and are now being tormented."
Sumitra:
Not only those who have gone to the forest, but even those who have gone to the world.
[Up to the end of verse 6.70, following the mention of "even that which has entered the world," there is *udvega* (agitation) due to the presentation of fear regarding the mother;
now follows *sambhrama* (confusion).]
Agitation (*sambhrama*) consists of apprehension and terror arising from enemies, tigers, and the like.
For example, in that same work (*Bālarāmāyaṇa*), Vāmadeva says (with tears, to himself):
"O my voice, release your own [throat]! Quickly, grant me passage outside."
(Aloud to the King) Your Majesty, steady yourself; a dry thunderbolt is falling upon your ears.
(The couple act out their apprehension. Vāmadeva:

Having received the command from you, Rāma— clad in robes, bearing a bow, with matted hair, and accompanied by the son of Sumitrā and Sītā— departed for the forest from some unknown place. Both fainted.
Vāmadeva: O King, take heart.
Daśaratha (having recovered): For what reason, he began.
Daśaratha: "My dear Rāmabhadra, I believe that this thorn of grief will consume even my dear friend Jaṭāyu, who dwells on Mount Malaya.

By this passage, ending with verse 6.55, the *sambhrama* (agitation) is expressed through the description of the persistence of fear and apprehension regarding Rāma’s exile among Kausalyā, Daśaratha, and others, amidst forests made dreadful by the roaming of *rākṣasas*, hyenas, tigers, and other wild beasts.
Now, as for *ākṣepa* (the sudden entrance):
"They define *ākṣepa* as the simultaneous introduction of the embryo and the seed. (SRs 3.119).
For example, in that same work (*Bālarāmāyaṇa*), in the fifth act, immediately after verse 5.74: (Entering with a sudden toss of the curtain, her name obscured and her face veiled...)
Śūrpaṇakhā (falling at his feet with a cry):
Noble brother, look! The crest-jewel of Tāṭakā has been plucked off;
the mass of flames from the submarine fire has been extinguished.
"O younger sister of the Ten-Necked One, a great calamity has occurred!
Noble brother, look! The crest-jewel of Takṣaka has been torn away, and the mass of flames from the submarine fire has been crushed."
"An imminent danger has arisen from the younger sister of the Ten-Necked One.
Having thus begun, Rāvaṇa (aloud):
—Then what of her? Śūrpaṇakhā: Even she, while claiming me to be suitable for the Lord of Laṅkā, has by them been made fit for the vow of a Kāpālika.

By this concluding passage, there is the figure of speech *ākṣepa* (anticipation), because the enthusiasm of Rāma— which was implicitly contained within the description of Rāvaṇa’s preeminence in eclipsing the splendor of all the gods by means of the portion [of the narrative] ending with the [mention of his] limbs— is now manifested through the form of the cutting off of Śūrpaṇakhā’s ears and nose. Now follows the *vimarśa-sandhi* (the juncture of deliberation).

That in which the meaning of the seed-syllable (*bījārtha*), having emerged from the womb [of the plot], is reflected upon through seduction, anger, calamity, and so forth, is called *vimarśa* (the juncture of reflection). // SRs 3.120 //
The arrangement of the constituent elements (aṅga) here is determined by their suitability for the attainment of the specific dramatic form (prakaraṇa).
Furthermore, there are the exceptions (apavāda), the clash (saṃpheṭa), and the powers of flight (vidrava) and dissolution (drava). // SRs 3.121 //

Splendor (dyuti), persistence (prasaṅga), deception (chalana), exertion (vyavasāya), obstruction (nirodhana), encouragement (prarocanā), agitation (vicalana), and acquisition (ādāna) constitute the thirteen [types of *nirvahaṇa-sandhi*]. 3.122.
Now, regarding *apavāda*:
therein, *apavāda* is said to be the proclamation of faults.
For example, in that same work, the *Bālarāmāyaṇa*, at the beginning of the eighth act titled *Vīravilāsa* (where two Rākṣasas enter).
"Friend Durmukha, something truly great is the collapse of Daśakaṇṭha’s spirit, in that even upon hearing of the slaying of Kumāra Siṃhanāda, he felt neither grief nor indignation.
Having begun thus, [he continues]:
"Alas! The Lord has offered a libation of water to his own modesty."
[How was the final libation of water offered by Your Majesty to the Goddess of Modesty?
[Immediately following verse 8.10, up to the end: because this proclaims the fault of Rāvaṇa’s wicked intent, it is *apavāda* (reproach).
Now, *saṃpheṭa* (the clash):
Speech composed of faults is declared to be *sampheṭa* (mutual abuse).
As in that same [work], Sumukha (*aside*): [text follows].
Friend Durmukha,
there is indeed an excess of valor on the part of Rāma’s younger brother, since he has sent this message to Prince Meghanāda as he sets out for Nikumbhilā:
"As long as the sacrificial oblation has not been consumed by the fire-god from the sacrificial ground of Nikumbhilā..."
Having obtained a chariot, arrows, a bow, and armor, you consider yourself invincible;

yet, even while the noble one is distressed by the agony of separation from Vaidehī, that Lakṣmaṇa—who has rendered his wrath toward Śakra’s conqueror fruitless—will soon defeat you. (Sundarakāṇḍa 3.125) [Bālakāṇḍa 8.15]
Having begun thus, [the action] occurs offstage:
"He who is dear to Sītā, who shattered the bow of the Lord, who slew Bālin, and who constructed the bridge across the ocean..."

Up to the verse, "Having slain Rāma— who is the slayer of demons, who desires victory, and who is terrifying— I shall worship your feet" (Bālarāmāyaṇa 8.47), there is *sampheṭa* (mutual confrontation) due to the recording of the angry words of Lakṣmaṇa, Indrajit, and Kumbhakarṇa.
Now, regarding *vidrava* (flight/disorder): "Conflict, slaughter, burning, and so forth are proclaimed as *vidrava*.

(SRs 3.127) As in that same work [after verse 8.48]: Sumukha says: "O King, Sumukha, a mere foot-soldier, considers that the son of Agni’s arrow has been discharged by Prince Meghanāda with the intent to incinerate Lakṣmaṇa."
Having begun with the word "saṃhitā," [it says] "(to the south) Sumukha": this is another application of caustic to a wound.
O Lord of Saumitri, you who have the tips of arrows aimed from a bow drawn back to the ear as your crest-jewel;
you who bear a trident in hand and possess a terrifying majesty with a fierce, loud, and tumultuous outburst of raucous laughter;
you who are meditated upon by the son of Sumitrā as a spreading, vast, and formidable host of Vetālas—[protect us].
And Indrajit was reduced to ashes by the flames issuing from his mouth.
(Rāvaṇa faints; everyone attends to him as is appropriate.
Rāvaṇa (acting out the cessation of his faint):

Up to this point, the *vidrava* (flight) is established through the narration of the agitation of the monkey army, the confinement of Sugrīva, the slaying of Kumbhakarṇa, the reduction of Indrajit to ashes, and the fainting of Rāvaṇa.
Now, regarding *drava* (distress):
"The sage Bharata, however, defines *drava* as the transgression against a superior. (SRs 3.129, 63a)

As it says in that very same place: Karaṅka—Fie upon your forest of arms, haughty with the intoxication of valor; fie upon your Candrahāsa sword; and fie upon those faces that once delighted the moon-crested Lord by severing the circle of his neck!
"In Kumbhakarṇa— who is gluttonous with excessive sleep and who daily indulges in long slumbers— hope remains for the revival of his long-forgotten weapons" (Bālarāmāyaṇa 8.74).
Here, *drava* (contempt) arises because a subordinate Rākṣasa is expressing derision toward his two masters, Daśakaṇṭha and Kumbhakarṇa.
Now, as for *śakti* (power):
the pacification of an arisen conflict is intended as *śakti*.
As in that very same work, in the ninth act named "The Slaying of Rāvaṇa" (prior to verse 9.49):
Purandara: Having begun with "The Lord Kālāgnirudra, in his task of burning the multitude of the Kulaparvatas," [the voice] from behind the scenes says:
"With the tips of his banner-staff marked by arrows, his charioteer fainting and bowing down..."

Frequented by rows of birds—vultures greedy for the taste of flesh—the chariot was led toward Laṅkā by horses whose neighing recalled their former status in the stable; its axle-tree was shattered by the falling of the great headless trunk (kabandha) of the Lord of the Rākṣasas. (Bālarāmāyaṇa 9.56)
By concluding with the statement that Rāvaṇa—the arch-enemy who was his adversary—has been utterly destroyed at the throat, there is a "power" (*śakti*) arising from the pacification of the conflict.
Now, regarding "splendor" (*dyuti*):
Splendor is defined by the wise as threatening and causing agitation. (SRs 3.133) 64a.
As in that same eighth act,
Rāvaṇa (looking upward):
"Is this assembly of gods hurrying away so very quickly?"
I suspect he takes pleasure in the ascetic's slaughter of a few rākṣasas.
(With angry menace) O gods, is this excessive joy of yours due to the killing of a mere petty demon?
Therefore, you have expanded yourselves to witness the prowess of my arms, which have conquered the world;
moreover, this very day Kumbhakarṇa, who delights in the taste of battle, is being awakened, and Meghanāda, the swift conqueror of the gods, is also being awakened by me. (Bālarāmāyaṇa 8.12)
Having begun thus, [the stage direction reads:
behind the scenes— "O heroes, pull down the gate-tower that must be dragged down in play; O fools, cast away the ten thousandfold sets of various weapons and armor!"
"Build the city gate so that it can pull down and cast down those who seize the playthings [of the children];
carry ten thousand [soldiers] equipped with various weapons and armor"—
by such statements ending here, which describe the threatening of the deities and the terrifying of the inhabitants of the city of Laṅkā, there is *dyuti* (splendor).
Now, as for *prasaṅga*: "The statement of a relevant matter is proclaimed as *prasaṅga*. (64b) Others describe *prasaṅga* as the praise of one's teachers. (SRs 3.135)

Just as in that very same ninth act [at the beginning], the servant of Yama enters and says: "The majesty of the Lord of Death, who bears the mark of a buffalo and whose destruction is ordained for all living beings, is something truly transcendent"—and after this introduction, Daśaratha says: "O Blessed Lord, Master of the Gods, may your glances be bestowed upon me here with favor."

[Up to the end of verse 9.18] *Prasaṅga* (incidental elaboration) occurs either through the mention of those worthy of worship, such as Yama and Purandara, or through the detailed expansion of the subject at hand, namely the slaughter of Rākṣasa.
Now, *chalanam* (deception):
"They know deception (*chalana*) to be the act of showing contempt and so forth for the sake of one's purpose" (SRs 3.136). 65.
[*18] In this *Nāṭyaśāstra*, the designation "covering" (*chādana*) is employed;
as in that very same work, the *Bālarāmāyaṇa*: the *cāraṇa* (listening to the air)—What does Rāmabhadra say?
O son of a Rākṣasa,
she by whom Jānakī was formerly beheld with eyes moist with love and full of graceful movement, having first performed the act of prostration at the lotus-feet of Gaurī!
"That head of yours has been severed, and this head of the Rākṣasa has arisen; your mind is now at peace.
But the method for cutting off the remainder is solely for my liberation from the celestial bards.
What did Rāvaṇa say?

Beginning with "O son of a Kṣatriya, you possess eyes of skin that are easily subject to delusion," and concluding with Rāma’s words, "Therefore, this impure mouth of yours must depart from here; let it find purification through death" (following verse 9.46), there is *chalanam* (deception) because Rāma and Rāvaṇa engage in mutual humiliation.
Now, *vyavasāya* (determination):
*Vyavasāya* is said to be the manifestation of one's own capability. As in that same work (*Bālarāmāyaṇa*): [text follows].
O Lord of Laṅkā, let Janakī be given; Rāma himself begs her.
What is this delusion of your mind? Remember the code of conduct; has nothing yet transpired?
If you do not, then [Rāma] will become mired in the blood from the throats of Khara, Dūṣaṇa, and Triśiras.
"O wretch! This shall not endure—the binding of my bowstring, which has been turned the color of the bandhūka flower.
Having begun thus, what did Rāvaṇa say? "Hey there, you son of a human woman!"
This is that Rāvaṇa, who is not a kṣatriya; this is Rāma, who is a kṣatriya. Let it be seen here.
"Who is the one to be disciplined?
Who is the discipliner?
What did Rāmabhadra say?
"O son of a non-human woman!
Rāma is a kṣatriya;
this Rāvaṇa is no kṣatriya at all."

In this regard, let it be seen that from the words "Which one is the disciple? Which one is the teacher? up to the end [of verse 9.26], there is *vyavasāya* (determination/resolution), because Rāma and Rāvaṇa proclaim their own respective capabilities.
Now, for *virodhana* (conflict):
*Virodhana* (conflict) is the expression of opposition among those who are enraged with one another.

For example, in that same work (*Bālarāmāyaṇa*), at that very place, a *cāraṇa* says: "How did the intolerant Rāma and Rāvaṇa proceed with a duel of showers of arrows?"—and having begun thus, the *cāraṇa* continues: "Is this not the syllable *Oṃ*, the spell for severing the circle of Rāvaṇa’s heads? [following verse 9.39].

Thus, at the end [of this], because Rāma and Rāvaṇa, being enraged, engage in a mutual obstruction consisting of the employment of divine missiles (*divyāstra*), there is *virodhana*. Now, regarding *prarocanā*: "A *prarocanā* would be the indication of a future matter as if it were already accomplished. (SRs 3.141) 67a.
As in that very same eighth act, immediately after verse 8.16:
Karaṅka (aside)—
Friend Kaṅkāla, His Majesty is awakening Kumbhakarṇa.
But not himself.
Moreover, even though he has been awakened with effort by Rāma, he must simply be laid down to sleep again.
Kaṅkāla: I believe this is the fate of everyone, with the exception of Vibhīṣaṇa.
"I think that this fate awaits everyone except Vibhīṣaṇa.
Karaṅka: "It is exactly so.
Here, *prarocanā* (the act of enticing) occurs because the future destruction of the Rākṣasas, such as Kumbhakarṇa, is indicated by Kaṅkāla and Karaṅka as if it were already accomplished.
Now, regarding wavering:
wavering is self-praise.
As in that same [text]: 67c.
Karaṅka: What does Kumbhakarṇa say? "Let the bow be; what need is there for the sword? Enough with the bhuśuṇḍī, the discus, the paṭṭiśa, the mallet, and the rest!"
"By devouring the hosts of rushing monkeys,
I shall attain both full satisfaction and the destruction of my enemies.
(Rāvaṇa asks again.)
"Excellent, my child, excellent!
You are truly my younger brother," he said,
beginning thus—
That Laṅkā, my city, was reduced to ashes by Hanumān, who had entered its very body—
this was surely done for the sake of pacifying his own offense.
"Even the Fire-god approaches me to serve me"—up to this point, Rāvaṇa and Kumbhakarṇa have performed self-praise; thus there is agitation (*vicalana*). Now, the taking hold (*ādāna*):
*Ādāna* is the gathering of the plot.

As in that same work, the *Bālarāmāyaṇa*, in the ninth act, Purandara says: "Friend Daśaratha, how is it that this heroic prowess of Rāmabhadra is without equal? And therefore—let Giriśa be the one who has already consumed the fuel of Tripura, while he [Rāma] is for the shattering of the Krauñca mountain!"
The wisdom of Guha was already known; what need was there for him who had not yet experienced the festival of battle?
Having cut down the forest of the Lord of Laṅkā—a hero whose deeds are marvelous to warriors—by means of the humiliation of his lotus-like army, Rāma stands at the ultimate limit. (Bālakāṇḍa 9.57)
Having begun thus:
"He, who wears garlands of mandāra flowers dropped by celestial women who delight in the passion of battle,
has himself descended here with his hand placed upon Lakṣmaṇa."
"Rāmabhadra, the beloved of the Fortune of the Solar Dynasty, [emerges] from the chariot, while bards utter cries of victory"—

up to this point is "Adāna" (the taking up), because it comprises the specific effects characterized by Dharma and so forth, accomplished through the slaying of Rāvaṇa, which serves to pacify the afflictions of the entire world.

Now, the *nirvahaṇa* juncture: where the *mukha*-juncture and the others, scattered throughout and joined with the seed (*bīja*), reach their great purpose—that is called the *nirvahaṇa*. (SRs 3.148) 68.

Junction (sandhi) and opposition (virodha), the tying together (grathana), the conclusion (nirṇaya), the consolation (paribhāṣaṇa), and the favoring (prasāda); likewise, joy (ānanda), convention (samaya), and composition (kṛti) [are used] in the embrace of speech (bhāṣopagūhana). 69.
Furthermore, prior existence (pūrvabhāva), association (sayuja), the summary (upasaṃhāra), and the eulogy (praśasti).
Thus they have described the components of the *nirvahaṇa* (conclusion); now I shall state their definitions.
Among them, *sandhi* (junction): the arrival of the seed (*bīja*) is *sandhi*.

As it occurs at the beginning of the tenth act of that same work, the *Bālarāmāyaṇa*, titled *Rāghavānanda*: (Then enters [Sītā], filled with grief: "O Laṅkā! O Durdhara! O Tava-viśeṣa! O Paritoṣita-aravinda-āsana! O sole champion of the three worlds, Daśakaṇṭha! O Meghanāda, who took Mahendra captive as if in play! O Kumbhakarṇa, who was so well-disposed toward the fury of battle! Where are you?"
Give me an answer!
[Alas, O Ten-necked One, sole champion of the three worlds, whose lotus-seated father was gratified by your extraordinary and difficult austerities;
alas, Meghanāda, who took Mahendra captive as if in sport!]
"Alas, O Kumbhakarṇa, who were so gracious in the fury of battle! Where are you? Give me an answer!"—with these words he began.
(Entering hurriedly) Alaka: Friend, even though Vibhīṣaṇa, the conqueror of Dharma, is now the leader, that noble lady remains as if pierced by the stake of grief.
The city of Laṅkā speaks of him who has only the eye of compassion.

The *sandhi* (junction) occurs because, ending with the words "[that which the city of the three-eyed friend speaks]" [prior to verse 10.2], the seed of Rāma’s resolve— consisting of the instruction of the wicked rākṣasa— is introduced. Now, for the *virodha* (contradiction):
The search for the effect would constitute a contradiction.
As in that very same [text], behind the scenes:
"O Rudrāṇī, Lakṣmī, Varuṇāṇī, Sarasvatī, Dyau!"
Sāvitrī, Dhātrī, and all the family deities,
along with the guardians of the worlds, quickly assemble and enter the fire for the sake of purification, together with the beloved of Rāma.
Having begun thus:
"O, even the gods and demons praise Sītā's side!
Or rather, everyone is fond of virtues."
"Not toward their bodies!
(Ah, even the deities show partiality toward Sītā!
Or rather, everyone is attached to virtues.)"
[Up to the end of verse 10.8, following the previous line: there is a contradiction because of the pursuit of the effect in the form of Sītā’s purification.
Now, the composition—
Stringing together is the insertion of that [comparison] therein;
as in that very same work, the *Bālarāmāyaṇa*:
"The bridge built over the salt ocean became fuel for the fire of his wrath."
The race of Rākṣasas has been subdued, and his pure wives have been recovered;
thus, now dwelling in the forest with his vow fulfilled, he fortunately proceeds to Ayodhyā by means of the Puṣpaka chariot for the pleasure of his beloved.
"O all you leaders of the monkey troops!"— beginning with these words,
Hanumān was dispatched to the side of Bharata, his splendor gazed upon by the startled eyes of the women of Laṅkā.
"Having demonstrated his essential prowess by crossing the ocean, he now departs for the accomplishment of the task appropriate for the time of the royal consecration"—
with these words, ending at *Bālarāmāyaṇa* 10.16, the composition concludes with the supreme act of disregarding Rāma’s consecration.
Now, the definition: Determination (*nirṇaya*) is the narration of what has been experienced.
As in that same work, the *Bālarāmāyaṇa*, Rāma (aside):
O fair-browed one, do you remember the water from the streams squeezed out by the hands of the venerable masters during the time of your sporting bath—
water which was fit only for an ornament for your own breasts?
Here, a petal from the lotus-stalk was given as a protective covering. Furthermore—there, on the sandy bank of the Narmadā, during their playful quarrels... [Bālarāmāyaṇa 10.76]

O fair-limbed one, do you remember that time when we slept under the power of another, and at dawn, the teacher’s task of swaying us with the breezes from the water was followed by the seal of passion and that firm embrace? (Śṛṅgāra-śataka 3.159; Bālarāmāyaṇa 10.77)
Thus, in this case, there is a *nirṇaya* (conclusive determination) because Rāma speaks of a matter he has personally experienced.
Now, regarding *paribhāṣā*:
*paribhāṣā* is mutual talk or else censure. (SRs 3.160) 72a

Just as in that very same place [immediately following verse 10.92]: Sītā: Noble son, by the mention of Vārāṇasī, you have caused me to remember Mithilā, that great city which was my mother and the delight of my eyes; O slayer of the Ten-necked one! Sītā: Noble son, by the mention of Vārāṇasī, you have caused me to remember Mithilā, that great city which was my mother and the delight of my eyes; O slayer of the Ten-necked one!
Having begun thus, Vibhīṣaṇa says: "Indeed, here has been granted a defeat to the sage Bhārgava, the destroyer of Kṣatriyas.
Sugrīva says:
"Having been satisfied by the foam of the waters and having bathed in the moonlight,
that sage has destroyed the Kṣatriya race whose skill remained unmanifest"—
ending with these words, there is a dialogue between Sītā, Rāma, Vibhīṣaṇa, and Sugrīva, or alternatively, a reproach arising from Sugrīva’s indication of Bhārgava’s censure.
Now, regarding *prasāda*:
they say that *prasāda* is the state of clarity (*prasannatva*) attained through such means as service (*śuśrūṣā*).
As it is said in that very same [text]: [72b]
Rāma (raising his hand):
O Puṣpaka! The smoke from the wind-swift speed of the sage is being swallowed up ahead;
do not cast a shadow, for someone stands here with fixed gaze upon the sun, the jewel of the day.
"O venerable one, perform a circumambulation here from a distance; this is the temple of Sthāṇu.
Stay for a moment until the ascetic returns from his journey before you. Having begun thus, Agastya says:
O scion of Raghu, what perfect blessing can be given to you, by whom the worlds have been rendered free of thorns?
Nevertheless, we pray that you may dwell together with your own heroes.
The daughter-in-law would have two sons resembling the Earth and Kāśyapa.

[Bālarāmāyaṇa 10.64] "Rāma has most graciously favored the Raghu dynasty"—up to this point, there is *prasāda* (grace), because of the description of the favor in the form of the blessing bestowed by Agastya. Now, *ānanda* (joy):

*svāmī*, *yuvrāja*, *kumāra*, and *bhartṛdāraka* denote a crown prince; *āvutta* denotes the husband of one's sister; and *syāla* denotes the commander of an army.
The term *bhaṭṭinī*, *svāminī*, *devī*, and likewise *bhaṭṭārikā* should be used by attendants when addressing women who are favorites of the king. (3.544)
The king should address his chief queen as "Devī," while others he may call "Priyā"; however, every wife should be addressed as "Āryā" by her husband using the name of her father or her son. (3.545)

A son should address his father as "tātapādāḥ" (father’s feet) and his mother as "mātāmbā" (mother-mother); likewise, he should address his elder brothers as "āryāḥ" (noble sirs), and similarly address his maternal uncles and others.
Now, the description of similar [terms]: A similar person should be addressed as "similar," or by the term "companion" (vayasya), or by the name [itself].
But a female friend (sakhi) should be addressed as "hala" by a female friend, or simply as "friend" (sakhi). (SRs 3.547)

Now follows the instruction regarding the youngest: indeed, younger ones—whether sons, disciples, or junior [relatives]—should be addressed by the elder with such designations as "child," "little son," "long-lived one," "dear one," or "born of [my] father. (SRs 3.548)
Another, being younger, is addressed by noble people with the titles of their craft or office, or as "Bhadra" or "Bhadramukha. (3.549)
When addressing those who are low or very low, one should use "haṇḍe" and "hañje" respectively;
servants should be addressed by their master using their own names or titles appropriate to their craft. (3.550)
In this manner, the application of the exposition should be employed; it is to be understood by those skilled in poetry as being consistent with both worldly convention and the treatises. 330.551.
Now, regarding the definition of names: even for a chamberlain or similar character whose name has not been mentioned, [the name should be used] when the plot is well-known;
however, when the plot is imaginary, it is clearly required even for the protagonist and other such characters. (3.552)
A poet should invent names suited to the aesthetic flavor (rasa) and the subject matter (vastu), such as Vinayandhara, Bābhravya, Jayandhara, Jaya, and so forth. (3.553)
The employment of chamberlains generally indicates a sign of trust, as does the use of objects such as creepers, ornaments, flowers, and other delicate things. (3.554)
One should assign names to the female attendants based on their established qualities;
for the male dependents, one may use names such as Karabha, Kalahaṃsa, and so forth. (3.555)
One should assign names such as Karpūra, Caṇḍa, and Kāmpilya to bards, and names such as Subuddhi and Vasubhūti to ministers. (3.556)
Devarāta and Somarāta were the names of two priests;
there were also Śrīvatsa, Gautama, Kautsa, Gārgya, and Maudgalya. (3.557)
The Vidūṣaka should be named Vasantaka or Kāpileya; he is distinguished by his majesty, heroism, victory, pride, valor, and daring. (3.558)
A learned person should give names to leaders of the *dhīrottarā* class using words such as *vasanta*, *bhūṣaṇa*, *uttaṃsa*, *śekhara*, and *aṅka*. (3.559)
"Candrāpīḍa" and "Kāmapāla" are names for those of graceful nature; "Ugravarmā" and "Caṇḍasena" are names for those of fierce disposition. (3.560)
A wise man should assign names ending in "Dattasena" for Vaiśyas;
such as Karpūramañjarī, Candralekhā, and Rāgataraṅgikā. (3.561)
Generally, the heroine (nāyikā) is to be addressed by names such as Padmāvatī;
however, queens (devī) are named Dhāriṇī, Lakṣmī, Vasumatī, and so forth. 3.562.
Bhogavatī, Kāntimatī, Kamalā, Kāmavallarī, Irāvatī, Haṃsapadī, and so forth are the names of Bhoginī. (3.563)
The Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas have names ending in *śarman*, *varman*, and *datta* respectively;
the lords of the Vidyādharas have names ending in *śikhaṇḍa*, *aṅgada*, and *cūḍā*. (3.564)
The Kāpālika people are known by names ending in *kuṇḍalānanda* and *ghaṇṭānta*; [the others are] Yogasundarikā, Vaṃśaprabhā, and Vikaṭamudrikā. (3.565)
The women of the Kāpālikas were known by such names as Śaṅkhakeyūrikā;
they were Ānandinī, Siddhimatī, Śrīmatī, and Sarvamaṅgalā. (3.566)

Having considered all such characteristics—such as a woman of good family (suvāsinī) whose name begins with "Yaśovatī," "Putravatī," and so forth—as set forth by one of perfected intellect: SRs 3.567.

A poem composed by a poet shines as long as the moon and sun endure, for those whose intellects are refined by the knowledge of constructing both the definitions and the illustrations [of poetic figures]. 3.568.
Let this work be examined with a mind free from envy.
The illustrious King Siṃha, a master of the Bharata-āgama and a connoisseur of aesthetic flavor, has thus composed the *Rasārṇavasudhākara*. 348–349.

When King Anapota-Siṃha, out of fury, marshaled his forces for an assault, the sounds of the kettledrums followed the resonance of "dhaṇaṃ dhaṇaṃ dhaṇam," while his veteran warriors rejoiced, crying out, "raṇaṃ raṇaṃ raṇam! (to battle! to battle! to battle!)
The rival kings fall into delusion, thinking "grass, grass,

grass," as they are placed one by one as counterweights upon the scale by the Creator, who— having considered the earth to be light when King Siṃhacandra was created— finds it exceedingly heavy once he is set there.

Although the sky was filled to its limits with circles fragrant from rows of wish-fulfilling trees and floods of *cintāmaṇi* jewels, it was yet further elevated by his hundreds of enemies through their own levity; even today, that heaven remains full of them.

Thus ends [the work] composed by the illustrious King Siṃha, whose arm-strength is terrifying, the son of the glorious King Anapota—the "Bhairava unto rival factions" and sovereign of the glorious Andhra region.
In the treatise on dramatic embellishments titled *Rasārṇava-sudhākara*, the third chapter, named "The Radiance of the Aesthetic Experience" (*bhāvakollāsa*), is concluded. //3//
And thus concludes this *Rasārṇava-sudhākara*.
May Hari— dwelling on the mountain of water (the ocean), dark as a tamāla tree,
and the auspicious autumnal moon to the cakora-birds that are the sages— be victorious!
The vast expanse of his stainless chest was smeared with the beauty of the saffron paste from the clusters of blossoms on the breasts of Lakṣmī.
The wind dwelling on the Malaya mountain, the moon with its cool rays, and the god of love whose fame is sanctified by his friends—
these wander for long somewhere, their forms unperceived even by elephants.
May that five-arrowed god, saluted by hosts of connoisseurs, be victorious!
May the succession of blessings from all those born of the twice-born cause auspiciousness to surge forth, and may the lifespan of poets be long.
